passages.t: ‘For Your sake we face death all day long’, and ‘Why are You sleeping?’
passages.happening:
This is a whole people praying, another Maskil of the sons of Korah. It moves in three steps.

First, memory. “We have heard with our ears, O God; our fathers have told us the work You did in their days, in the days of old” (verse 1). The land was not won by their own strength: “It was by Your right hand, Your arm, and the light of Your face” (verse 3). So they still trust God, not weapons. “For I do not trust in my bow, nor does my sword save me” (verse 6).

Then a shock. “But You have rejected and humbled us; You no longer go forth with our armies” (verse 9). They have lost a war. They are scattered and mocked. “You sell Your people for nothing” (verse 12).

Then the protest. “All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten You or betrayed Your covenant” (verse 17). “Yet for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered” (verse 22).

It ends with the boldest words in the psalm. “Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping? Arise! Do not reject us forever” (verse 23). “Redeem us on account of Your loving devotion” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world a lost battle was read as a verdict. If a people lost, others assumed their god was weak or angry with them. So defeat brought shame as well as death. That is why the psalm speaks of being “a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples” (verse 14).

No event is named. Readers have suggested many: wars in the time of the kings, the Assyrian invasions, the exile to Babylon. The psalm does not say, and that has let people pray it after every disaster since.

‘Spread out our hands’ (verse 20) was the way people prayed, arms lifted. To spread them to a foreign god was to worship an idol. The people say they have not done that.

To tell God to wake up was daring. Elijah had mocked the god Baal for perhaps sleeping (1 Kings 18:27). Another psalm says, “the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4). The singers knew that. Their cry says how things feel, not what they think God is.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 22 in one of the great chapters of the New Testament. He asks, “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” He names trouble, danger and sword, and then quotes this psalm (Romans 8:35-36). His answer: “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). Paul does not deny the suffering. He says it cannot cut believers off from God's love.

The disciples once woke Jesus in a storm with a cry like verse 23: “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38).
passages.hard:
Does the Bible not say that faithfulness brings blessing? Deuteronomy does promise blessing for obedience, and the prophets often explain Israel's disasters as judgment for sin. But this psalm says plainly that this time the people had been faithful, and they suffered anyway. It does not claim they were sinless. It claims they had not turned away from God.

So suffering is not always punishment. The book of Job says the same, and so did Jesus about a man born blind (John 9:3). The psalm leaves its question open, and God kept it in Scripture that way. The book page lists this verse among the hard passages of the Psalms.
passages.asks:
This psalm gives you permission to argue with God when you have tried to be faithful and life has still fallen apart. It does not turn its back on God. Every line is spoken to him.

Notice the last words. They do not ask God to act because the people deserve it. They ask on account of his ‘loving devotion’, his hesed, the love that keeps its promises. When you cannot see why you are suffering, that is still ground you can stand on.
